newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi rejects Amnesty report of refugee killings.
newsitem.headline: Burundi rejects Amnesty report of refugee killings.

text.p: Burundi's military government on Thursday rejected accusations by Amnesty International that up to 500 Hutu refugees had been killed by its security forces after returning from eastern Zaire in recent weeks.
A spokesman for Burundian military leader Pierre Buyoya, who came to power on July 25 in a coup, said the London-based human rights group was tarnishing its reputation through propaganda.
Amnesty called on the United Nations to ensure the safety of returnees, saying thousands faced fresh atrocities at the hands of the army.
"No refugees should be forcibly returned to a country which has seen as many 500 returnees reportedly killed by the Burundi security forces in recent weeks," Amnesty said in a statement.
"It is completely unacceptable for governments to remain silent and refuse to condemn this appalling situation," it added.
Amnesty said it had documented cases of killings, disappearances and ill-treatment occurring almost daily among the returning refugees, with women, children, babies and the elderly among the victims.

But Jean-Luc Ndizeye, a spokesman for military leader Pierre Buyoya, told Reuters: "This (report) is completely false information and it is not the first time that Amnesty has done this sort of thing. It calls their credibility into question."
"We have called for an increase in human rights monitors and we have talked to people here about these reports of disappearances," he added.
At least 400 returnees were rounded up at a church in Muramba in the region of Cibitoke and the adult males were shot or bayoneted on October 22, Amnesty said in one example of abuses.

The report follows a human rights furore caused by the discovery of at least 33 bodies of men, women and children -- many with their hands tied suggesting execution -- at the mouth of the Rusizi river this month.

Aid workers and diplomats said up to 140 Burundian Hutu males and their families were massacred by the Tutsi-dominated army screening returning refugees for suspected Hutu rebels, and their bodies were dumped in the Rusizi.
Around 35,000 Burundian Hutus who fled camps north of South Kivu's Uvira town in Zaire last month have returned to Burundi, most of them crossing into the troubled north west Cibitoke region.

The influx has been overshadowed by the return home of 500,000 Rwandan Hutus from camps around Goma in North Kivu between November 15 and 19. Some 700,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees remain missing, according to U.N. refugee agency figures.
Around 140,000 Burundian Hutu refugees fled Uvira camps with 90,000 Rwandan refugees last month after fighting between Zairean rebels who now control much of east Zaire and the Zairean army.

In August Amnesty said Burundi's army killed more than 4,000 unarmed civilians in central Gitega region in the three weeks after the coup, but analysts said that report damaged the organisation's credibility.
The report was denied by the military government and disputed by the U.N. and Burundian human rights organisations who said no more than 400 were killed in Gitega.
Around 150,000 people -- mainly civilians -- have died in the past three years in a civil war after Burundi's first elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted coup by Tutsi soldiers.
East African states imposed economic and transport sanctions six days after the July coup.

Diplomats report an upsurge of fighting after Hutu rebels from the Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD) started crossing the country heading for Tanzania after the fall of the Uvira camps in Zaire.
